Imagine a thousand people. Each has a different amount of talent, and all of them start with the same ten units of money.
Every six months, chance rolls past them. Green balls are lucky breaks. Red balls are bad luck.
When a green ball comes by, talent matters. A talented person is more likely to grab it, and their money doubles.
When a red ball comes by, talent doesn't help at all. Their money is cut in half.
Run this for forty years, and the money ends up lopsided. The richest fifth hold about eighty percent of it.
So who ends up on top? Usually not the most talented. In the researchers' own run, the richest person's talent was zero point six one, barely above average.
The most talented person, at zero point eight nine, ended with less than they started with.
Over ten thousand runs, the winners averaged just zero point six seven. Talent helps. Luck decides.
That matters for how we hand out rewards. Give money to whoever is already successful, and you mostly reward the lucky.
In the model, giving everyone a small, equal share worked better. It more than doubled the number of talented people who got ahead.
Talent is necessary. It just isn't enough. You also need a few green balls.
